svg.text: Глава 32. Краткая история системного администрирования — итоговая timeline
operators • time-sharing • UNIX • BSD • profession • Linux • Windows • cloud • IoT

text.tspan: Expensive computers begin as specialized systems.
Operators maintain the machine/workload.
IBM user communities exchange experience/programs.
Time-sharing turns computers into shared platforms.
Administration scope starts to broaden.
Bell Labs leaves Multics.
A smaller interactive system evolves on PDP-7.
By 1971 UNIX has a growing utility set.
By 1973 the chapter highlights C and pipes.
Composition becomes a defining property.
Do one task well.
Build programs that work together.
Use text streams as a common interface.
Pipe: one program output → another input.
Power comes from relationships between tools.
Academic publication expands adoption.
Berkeley work evolves into BSD.
Documentation helps others understand the system.
TCP/IP sockets extend network capability.
SunOS and System V broaden commercial use.
General-purpose UNIX needs broad operational skills.
Universities become training/community centers.
Admins create tools, standards and procedures.
Role spans hardware, users, storage and troubleshooting.
Evi Nemeth is presented as a major community figure.
Professionalization creates demand for practical docs.
Books, conferences and peer networks scale knowledge.
Chapter mentions O'Reilly, LISA and SANS.
First handbook edition appears in 1989.
Current organization/event status needs confirmation.
Commodity PCs make broad deployment practical.
Linux emerges during BSD legal uncertainty.
Windows becomes a major server platform.
Later operations become increasingly multi-platform.
Book-era TCO claims are historical context only.
Virtualization and cloud change the unit of administration.
Infrastructure can be created through APIs.
Standardization, automation and monitoring become core.
Administrator skills expand to DevOps and large fleets.
Operational calm still matters during mass failure.
IoT extends the number and variety of managed systems.
Small devices still need security, performance and availability.
Publication-era IoT forecasts are not verified outcomes.
Platforms change; systems still need stewardship.
Reliability + users + troubleshooting + learning remain.

svg.text: Core: system administration evolves by scale and platform, not by abandoning its operational fundamentals.
Community knowledge and composable tools are recurring force multipliers.
